BEFORE YOU BEGIN

This is a book about making a game with GPT-6 Astra. Signal Garden is the worked design example; the prompts and milestones are original templates, not a claim that the game has already been built or benchmarked.

QUICK READ

Quick summary

The main points and the shortest path through the book.

  • Start small: one playable loop with clear completion rules.
  • Add only useful guidance: skills can help, but availability does not guarantee correct selection or better results.
  • Judge the result: play it, record evidence, and improve one cause at a time.

The concise steps

  1. Define the game. Write the objective, controls, win/loss rules, and exclusions. The working loop → · Full game brief →
  2. Choose a manageable approach. Match the workflow and engine to your biggest unknown; test a tiny browser export. Compare approaches → · Choose the stack →
  3. Check the evidence. Match advice to the model and installed versions. Non-Astra benchmarks do not prove Astra gains. Research method →
  4. Give the project a memory. Save the brief, acceptance checks, commands, and progress in Git; review changes before committing. Repository setup →
  5. Check tools and skills. Reuse relevant available guidance; add a skill only for a demonstrated gap. MCP connects capabilities; hooks respond to events. Skill decisions → · Decision and data flows →
  6. Give Astra a focused request. Use the compact prompt with accurate project files, or the bootstrap for an empty folder. A meta-prompt is optional. Execution prompts → · Prompt designer →
  7. Build in playable stages. Setup → movement → win loop → loss/challenge → visual polish → release checks. M0–M5 plan →
  8. Verify real play. Test controls, collision, pause, win, loss, and restart. Observe a human playtest. Full verification guide →
  9. Fix, then distill. Save prompts and outcomes, repair the cause, and retain verified lessons. Compare P1/P2 from the same baseline before claiming a better prompt. Refinement method →
  10. Publish and check. Build for the repository subpath, deploy when authorized, then verify the expected revision and a complete run at the public URL. GitHub Pages walkthrough →
  11. Optional: make a trailer. Use real capture for gameplay, label generated concepts, compose the clips, and review the final export. Video workflow →

Signal Garden and these workflows are worked proposals, not measured game results. Source summaries → · Review and evidence limits →

CHAPTER 01

The better loop

A better result begins with a smaller uncertainty.

You ask an AI agent to make a beautiful 3D game. It creates a landscape, a character, a menu, and several hundred lines of code. The screenshot looks promising. Then you press a key: the camera points into a wall, the player slides through a collectible, and nothing explains how to win. The request was easy to begin and difficult to finish because “good” never became something you could observe.

This book uses one original example, Signal Garden: guide a small maintenance robot around an abandoned rooftop garden, collect three energy cells, avoid a patrolling drone, and power a beacon before time runs out. The game is deliberately small. It gives us enough movement, collision, feedback, atmosphere, and state transitions to practice making a complete experience.

01 / INTENTDescribeWhat should a player experience?
02 / ACTIONBuildMake one part playable.
03 / EVIDENCEObservePlay it. Capture what happens.
04 / LEARNINGRefineChange the weakest part.

Give every iteration a question

“Can a new player find the beacon?” is a useful question. It suggests a route, a camera angle, a first playtest, and a way to judge the change. “Make the game more professional” leaves the agent to guess among textures, controls, menus, sound, or architecture. The next step is often easier to choose when the current problem is named precisely.

For this book, better means increasing the quality of the player’s experience while keeping the cost of the next change manageable. The first half needs playtesting. The second needs understandable files, repeatable checks, and recoverable commits. A beautiful frame and a successful build each answer only part of the question.

A model, an agent, and a workflow

GPT-6 Astra is the requested model. An agent is the surrounding software that gives that model access to files, a terminal, documentation, and possibly a browser or game editor. A workflow is your agreement about what to build, what evidence to collect, and when to continue. A pasted prompt cannot give an ordinary chat tools it does not have.

OpenAI’s Astra guidance recommends making autonomy, instruction-file behavior, delegation, and test scope explicit. Use the model name shown by your agent host, and check that the tools needed for the task are available. The game recipe here does not depend on a particular subscription tier or an invented model capability. [01]

The working principle

Write the smallest instruction that carries the intent, constraints, and evidence needed for the next useful decision.

How to use this book

Read the approach comparison before choosing an engine. Set up the repository and fill the game brief. Use a compact execution prompt when the brief is clear; use the optional meta-prompt to resolve missing design decisions. Review available skills before adding project-specific instructions. Build through useful checkpoints, keep the evidence, and revise the workflow when the model or the task changes.

The September 2026 revision checks the advice against current Astra guidance and research published or updated since March. Every source has a readable summary, date information, and limits in the reading notes. Older videos remain explicitly labeled background.

For a visual map, use the thinking, decision, and improvement diagrams. The video walkthrough extends the same method to a game trailer and explains how node workflows, MCP, skills, and hooks fit together.

Try this before you prompt

Write one sentence for the player’s objective, one action that should feel satisfying, and one observable condition that means the first version is done. If those sentences are unclear, work on the game idea first.

CHAPTER 02

Six ways to build

Choose an approach for the uncertainty you have.

There is no single best prompting style for every stage of a game. A fast sketch helps you discover a direction. A specification helps you preserve a direction. A test helps you check a claim. Confusion begins when one of those activities is expected to do all three.

The comparison below is an editorial assessment for a solo developer making a small browser game. It is not a measured ranking of models. Setup effort and review effort depend on the project and the tools the agent can actually use.

ApproachBest useMain weaknessRefinement
1. One-shot prototypeDiscover an attractive visual or a promising mechanic quickly.A broad request can hide incomplete controls and game states.Limit it to one arena and one loop. Treat it as a sketch until you play it.
2. Specification firstPreserve a clear idea across many changes.Documentation can grow before the game has proved enjoyable.Write a one-page brief and a short acceptance list; validate with a playable slice.
3. Tutorial guidedLearn an unfamiliar engine using a known example.Old APIs, incompatible assets, or copied structure can mislead.Match versions, reproduce the small lesson, then adapt one mechanic.
4. Incremental agent loopBuild a complete game over several sessions.Local improvements can drift from the whole experience.Keep a runnable baseline, milestone evidence, and a short handoff note.
5. Visual playtest loopImprove camera, readability, animation, and feedback.A good screenshot does not prove behavior over time.Pair images with actual input sequences and state observations.
6. Parallel specialistsIndependent research, art exploration, or review of stable interfaces.Conflicting edits and integration can consume the time saved.Assign separate files or read-only work; one owner integrates and tests.

What the sources establish

GitHub’s Spec Kit separates specification, planning, tasks, and implementation. That is a useful model for keeping intent visible. It does not require a tiny game to adopt every template or tool in the kit. [06]

Anthropic reports that long-running web-app agents benefited from incremental work, progress records, Git history, and browser verification. Its report does not establish that multiple agents always beat a single agent, or that its findings automatically transfer to every game. [05]

Its March 2026 follow-up revisits the surrounding workflow as models improve. Treat elaborate planning structures as experiments to justify, not prerequisites. Our milestone list names visible outcomes; it does not require a separate agent or a rigid planning ceremony for each one. [21]

OpenAI’s Astra game case study combines a player-experience brief, concept references, inspectable state, repeatable scenes, and tests using real controls. It provides an implementation example, rather than a controlled comparison of these six approaches. [04]

The recommended combination

For Signal Garden, begin with a small specification, use a tutorial only where engine knowledge is missing, and make the first complete loop with one agent. Add visual review immediately after movement works. Introduce parallel work only when there is a task that can be integrated without changing the game’s shared assumptions.

A useful delegation might be: “Review the collision module without editing it, and report reproducible failures.” A poor split is: “One agent builds movement while another rewrites the camera and a third redesigns the coordinate system.” Those tasks depend on one another even if their file names differ.

Decision rule

If you do not know whether the idea is fun, prototype it. If you know what should happen but the agent keeps drifting, improve the specification. If you do not know whether it works, improve the evidence.

Choose a first experiment

Write the biggest unknown in your game. Pick one row of the comparison to address it. Name the artifact that will let you decide what to do next: a playable build, a control test, a reference image, or a one-page decision.

CHAPTER 03

Learn from the evidence

A transcript becomes useful when it changes a decision.

Searching for “best AI game prompt” produces demonstrations, tool promotions, speculative claims, and genuine engineering advice side by side. Read each source for a specific purpose. Use engine documentation to establish API behavior. Use a creator’s demonstration to learn a process. Use your own build to find out whether that process works under your constraints.

Start with the current evidence

This revision prioritizes material published or updated from 1 March through 14 September 2026. The two September OpenAI articles directly address Astra; the newer skill studies test other models and therefore inform hypotheses, not claims of Astra performance. Live official documentation is retained even when it exposes no publication date. A page checked today is not necessarily an article written today.

For the skills question, begin with the Astra instruction audit, then compare SWE-Skills-Bench with SkillsBench’s July update. Read SkillsInjector for selection and SkillAlchemy for evidence-led generation. Each entry below has main-item summaries and tested-model limitations.

Earlier ideaSeptember 2026 assessmentWhat changes in this book
Break long work into recoverable pieces.Still a useful project practice; the amount of external scaffolding should be reassessed as models improve. [21]Use outcome checkpoints, and let implementation order adapt to dependencies.
Give the agent more context.Useful context remains important; requiring every document for every edit is excessive for Astra. [17]Point to documents by purpose and avoid duplicating the full brief.
Create a skill to improve the project.Conditional. Existing skills may suffice; studies differ by skill quality, task, and model. [18] [22]Custom skill creation becomes optional, with a comparison against the current setup.
Verify the generated result.Still supported by current Astra game practice. [04]Keep behavior and visual evidence; use focused checks rather than repetitive blanket demands.
Generate a detailed prompt before coding.No reviewed experiment establishes that a meta-prompt always outperforms a direct request on Astra.Use it to resolve uncertainty; offer a compact prompt when the brief already exists.
Follow tutorial export instructions.Version and hosting constraints remain real despite better models. [11] [12]Check current engine documentation and test the actual deployment path.

Why keep any older videos?

The 2025 videos below are historical exceptions. The verification passage in Software Is Changing (Again) was checked again; the other transcript could not be retrieved in this review. Neither is current product documentation or an Astra benchmark. Recent video searches did not yield a verified replacement transcript suitable for these notes.

Transcript notebook: Software Is Changing (Again)

In his Y Combinator keynote, Andrej Karpathy discusses the loop between AI generation and human verification. He argues that concrete requests and auditable intermediate artifacts make that loop more useful, and notes that a huge code diff still leaves substantial review work. These are conceptual observations, not measured results for game production. [02]

Our application: ask for one runnable game milestone with a short list of behaviors to inspect. Put the build link, relevant change, and evidence together. The person reviewing the game should be able to answer a question such as “Does losing all health always show a restart screen?” without first reconstructing the agent’s entire conversation.

Transcript notebook: How I use LLMs

Retrieval limitation: the previous edition’s note used a public transcript mirror. That mirror timed out during this review, and an alternative returned a video landing page without transcript text. The former passage summary is therefore withdrawn from this edition’s verified evidence. The original video remains a historical reading lead. [03]

Our application: attach the actual error, installed engine version, current scene structure, and a relevant documentation excerpt to a debugging request. “The player is broken” supplies almost no useful working information. “In Godot version X, this CharacterBody3D falls through the floor in this minimal scene” gives the agent an investigation it can carry out.

The recommendation to supply relevant current evidence is supported independently by Astra’s current guidance on loading task-relevant context. It does not depend on the unavailable transcript. [17]

Transcript provenance

Source 02 uses a public transcript mirror of the original speech; automatic captions may contain errors. No stable passage timestamps were available, so the note gives a searchable term. Source 03 is a reading lead with unavailable transcript evidence. A reachable page or video title does not verify its spoken content.

A game tutorial is a separate kind of evidence

GDQuest’s written Godot 4 course and Godot’s own first-3D-game tutorial provide a sequence for learning game structure. Use them to reduce unfamiliarity with the engine. The GDQuest YouTube transcript could not be retrieved reliably during research, so only its accessible written course is used here. [09] [10]

Do not carry an entire tutorial into a new design unchanged. Extract one concept, such as movement relative to the camera. Build a minimal reproduction with the installed engine version. Then explain how the concept maps to your game, including what must change. A successful exercise is evidence that you understand one part; it does not validate the whole game.

A repeatable research procedure

  1. Start with a question. For example: “Can the chosen Godot export run on GitHub Pages without custom response headers?”
  2. Find the primary answer. Search official documentation for the installed version; open the page and read the constraints.
  3. Find an applied example. Prefer a creator’s video with an accessible transcript and companion repository.
  4. Record provenance. Save the URL, title, retrieval date, version, and a passage locator. Mark missing captions or an unavailable repository explicitly.
  5. Separate observation from inference. “The tutorial uses this node” is an observation. “This will simplify our camera system” is a hypothesis.
  6. Run one small experiment. Keep the result and the code commit that produced it.
Question: Will the beacon remain visible behind the planter?
Source: [official API link or creator's original tutorial]
Version / date: [installed version] / [date reviewed]
Observed idea: [brief paraphrase]
Our hypothesis: [how it may help this game]
Experiment: [small reproducible change]
Outcome: [measured result, or NOT TESTED]
Commit: [actual revision]

Two accounts of the same video are one underlying source. A successful edited demonstration does not reveal the unsuccessful runs, total effort, or hidden manual work. Keep the useful method, and test the outcome yourself.

CHAPTER 04

Choose the right workspace

Pick the stack your agent can build and you can judge.

The game’s delivery platform should influence the engine choice early. For a small game intended to live at a GitHub Pages URL, a browser-native stack offers a direct path from code changes to a playable link. For an existing Godot or Unity project, preserving the engine may be more useful than switching to match a fashionable workflow.

StackWhat you getWhat you still ownChoose it when…
TypeScript + Vite + Three.jsA code-oriented 3D rendering workflow and a small static-site deployment path. [12] [14]Gameplay architecture, movement, collisions, input, UI, and asset management.Your game is small, browser delivery matters, and your agent can edit and run code.
Babylon.jsA browser 3D engine with a broad feature set, including physics integration and inspection tools. [15]Game design, integration choices, compatibility checks, and performance tuning.You want more engine facilities within a JavaScript workflow.
Godot + GDScriptScenes, nodes, a visual editor, and an established beginner learning path. [09]Editor access or clear scene-file conventions; a tested web export configuration.You prefer an engine workflow or plan native game releases too.
UnityAn editor-centered game project that can target supported web browsers. [16]The installed editor and modules, asset import workflow, and web-build testing.You already know Unity or need an existing project and its assets.

These are practical selection criteria, not benchmark results or a complete feature comparison. Test the cheapest risky part before committing to the stack. If the agent cannot reliably inspect the editor, begin with a tiny scene and an export test to discover that limitation immediately.

Our default: Three.js, TypeScript, and Vite

Signal Garden uses a fixed, slightly elevated camera, a flat arena, simple geometric obstacles, and a small number of moving objects. That scope makes a browser codebase a reasonable teaching choice. Start with simple collision shapes and a readable state machine. If the design later depends on slopes, rigid-body interactions, or complex character movement, evaluate an appropriate physics solution before improvising one.

Use compatible stable package versions available when you start, commit the lockfile, and record the versions in the README. Use npm ci for a clean install from a matching committed lockfile; it fails on a package/lock mismatch rather than silently updating the lock. Avoid copying an old tutorial’s versions without checking compatibility. Demonstrate the chosen renderer on the target browsers. [42]

If you choose Godot instead

For a straightforward Pages release, begin by testing a GDScript project with Compatibility rendering and a single-thread web export. Godot’s documentation states that web exports use WebGL 2, that Godot 4 C# projects currently cannot export to web, and that threaded exports require cross-origin isolation. These are version-sensitive constraints. [11]

Prove an empty scene’s exported build loads at the final project URL before building a full game. Keep the export files together. The HTML entry can be named index.html; keep the other generated files’ names unchanged. Godot also documents a PWA service-worker workaround for isolation, so the single-thread recommendation is a simple starting route, not proof that every threaded Pages deployment is impossible. [11]

Export naming: choose index.html in the export dialog itself. Do not rename the generated HTML or companion files afterward; their references depend on the original export name. [11]

The 30-minute feasibility check

As a timeboxed exercise, create a floor, one object, and a camera. Make the object move, build the output, and serve it under a repository subpath. Record what failed. The timebox is a planning suggestion, not a promised completion time.

CHAPTER 05

Give the work a memory

The repository is the handoff between yesterday and tomorrow.

Git records local history. GitHub holds a remote copy, review conversations, issues, and automation. GitHub Pages serves the published game or book. Keeping those roles separate makes debugging easier: a local commit is not a push, a push is not a successful deployment, and a deployment is not proof that the game is playable.

Step 1: establish a clean starting point

In a new empty game folder, initialize Git on main. If the folder is already a repository, inspect its status and preserve the current work instead. Install Git and GitHub CLI, and authenticate GitHub CLI before creating a remote. The following commands are an example for a new Signal Garden project; replace the account name first. [39] [40]

git init -b main
git status --short
# Create the README, .gitignore, game brief, and project files.
# Review ignore rules and all scaffolded files before staging.
git status --short
git add --all
git diff --cached --stat
git diff --cached
git commit -m "chore: establish the Signal Garden baseline"
gh repo create YOUR_ACCOUNT/signal-garden --public --source=. --remote=origin
git push -u origin main

In this new project, stage the complete scaffold, including index.html, configuration files, and required assets. The two diff commands show its file summary and actual staged content. Set ignore rules for dependencies, local environment files, and build output as appropriate before staging. In an existing repository, stage only the intended paths so unrelated work stays separate. A public repository and Pages site publish the selected files; keep credentials and unlicensed assets out of the commit. [39]

Step 2: keep the important decisions in files

signal-garden/
  AGENTS.md                     # Optional short project conventions
  .agents/skills/signal-garden-round-review/
    SKILL.md                    # Optional; only if it adds proven value
  docs/
    game-brief.md               # Player promise and constraints
    acceptance.md               # Observable completion conditions
    decisions.md                # Choices and reasons
    progress.md                 # Current state and next step
    playtests/                  # Human observations and evidence links
  src/
    game/                       # State, input, simulation
    render/                     # Scene, camera, visual feedback
    ui/                         # Instructions, HUD, result screens
  public/assets/
    credits.md                  # Asset provenance and license notes
  tests/                        # Focused behavior checks
  .github/workflows/pages.yml
  package.json
  package-lock.json

This structure is a starting proposal, not a demand to create empty abstractions. A tiny build can begin with fewer modules. Separate systems when their responsibilities become clear, especially if simulation logic is difficult to test because it is mixed with rendering code.

Step 3: make a checkpoint per meaningful change

A useful commit says what behavior now works: feat: collect cells and power the beacon is better than update. Save a known working baseline before trying an uncertain idea. This example improves readability while preserving Signal Garden’s fixed camera. The switch reference documents creating its branch. Create the named playtest file with your observations, and adapt the paths to the actual project. [39]

git switch -c experiment/camera-readability
# Adjust the fixed camera framing, then playtest the obstructed route.
git diff
git add src/render/camera.ts docs/playtests/camera-readability.md
git diff --cached
git commit -m "fix: keep the robot visible behind the north planter"
git push -u origin experiment/camera-readability
# Write docs/pr-camera.md with the problem, change, and checks first.
gh pr create --base main --head experiment/camera-readability --title "Improve fixed camera readability" --body-file docs/pr-camera.md

The --body-file option reads an existing file; it does not create the description for you. The PR should state the player-visible problem, change, and checks. For a solo experiment, a branch and reviewed commit may be enough. Use a PR when review or CI gates add value. [41]

Step 4: leave a short continuation note

At the end of a session, update progress.md with the current commit, working behavior, known failure, launch command, and one next milestone. Anthropic’s long-running-agent report uses progress artifacts and Git history to reduce the need for a new session to reconstruct previous work. [05]

When a bad change has already been shared, git revert creates a new commit that undoes it while preserving history. Inspect dependencies between commits and resolve any conflicts before completing the revert. For an uncommitted experiment, show the exact diff and restore only the intended changes; unrelated work may be present. [39]

CHAPTER 06

Decide whether a skill adds value

Start with what the agent already has. Add what the task is missing.

The claim that project skills can be redundant is partly supported. A skill that repeats general coding advice may contribute little, while a specific workflow can supply knowledge the agent lacks. Automatic skill selection is a capability to use and evaluate; it is not evidence that the agent always selects correctly or produces a better game.

For visual guidance, see the decision graph for choosing tools, skills, and hooks. The video chapter adds a current example: Remotion has deprecated its older documentation MCP in favor of skills, while Comfy exposes MCP tools that execute media workflows. [27] [37]

Astra update · 11 September 2026

OpenAI recommends reassessing accumulated instructions for Astra. Overspecified procedures and overlapping skill descriptions can impede useful work. The practical change here is to make custom skills optional, with a specific reason to exist. This is guidance, not a measured Astra skill benchmark. [17]

Four different things people call “adding a skill”

  1. Make a skill available. Install or expose it to the agent’s host. A file elsewhere on the internet is not automatically available.
  2. Let the agent select it. Codex supports implicit matching between a task and an available skill’s description. Explicit selection is also supported. [08]
  3. Write a new skill. Package a missing reusable procedure, references, or scripts. This is a separate decision from invoking an existing one.
  4. Write repository instructions. AGENTS.md supplies scoped conventions; it is not an on-demand skill selector. [07]

Check the claims, one by one

Implicit selection also depends on host configuration. In Codex, allow_implicit_invocation: false disables automatic invocation for that skill. A crowded initial catalog can shorten or omit entries under its context budget. Check availability, eligibility, and what was actually invoked before attributing a result to skill quality. [08]

ClaimEvidence-based verdictDecision for Signal Garden
Every project needs a custom skill.Not established. Software-task results show that many tested skills added no benefit. [22]Begin with the brief, working tools, and existing available skills.
The agent can call the correct skill itself.Implicit selection is documented; reliable selection on every task is not guaranteed. [08]Check whether the relevant skill was available and actually used when diagnosing a failure.
Automatically calling a skill is always better than mentioning it.No direct Astra comparison was found in the reviewed sources.Try explicit selection when the right available skill was missed; compare outcomes.
Astra makes all skills obsolete.Unsupported. Current Astra guidance still identifies uses for specialized workflows. [17]Keep unique project knowledge or useful scripts when they earn their maintenance cost.
More skills mean more capability.Selection and context interactions matter; more is not consistently better. [19]Remove duplicate or overly broad optional entries and evaluate again.
AI-generated skills never help.Too broad. SkillAlchemy reports gains from an evidence-led generation method on other models. [20]Validate a generated procedure before adopting it; do not assume it improves Astra.

Why the studies seem to disagree

SWE-Skills-Bench found little average benefit from public software skills using Haiku 4.5. SkillsBench reports larger gains for curated skills across a broader task mix. Those are different interventions, tasks, and agent configurations. They can both be true. Neither answers whether this particular game-review skill helps Astra. [22] [18]

Our recommendation: do not create a new skill merely because a tutorial includes that step. First let Astra attempt a bounded task with the information already available. If it misses an existing procedure, inspect selection. If it lacks a recurring piece of project knowledge, supply that knowledge. A prompt correction, a documentation update, or a small script may be sufficient.

A compact AGENTS.md for the example game

The task prompt names the immediate outcome. The game brief owns the game rules. AGENTS.md can map recurring decisions to the relevant documents and commands. Keeping each fact in one place makes later changes easier to maintain.

READY TO USE · agents-example.md
# Signal Garden — project instructions

Project references: docs/game-brief.md defines mechanics and scope; docs/acceptance.md defines observable behavior; docs/progress.md records the current milestone and known issues. Consult the documents relevant to the task. Preserve existing user work.

Use TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js with the committed lockfile. Keep Y as up, movement on X/Z, and speed in world units per second. Prefer a small clear module over a new abstraction without a present need.

Commands after scaffolding: npm run dev, npm run build, npm test. Keep these scripts accurate in package.json and the README.

Keep simulation state separate from scene objects where that makes behavior easier to inspect. Put tunable gameplay constants in one named configuration module.

Verify the behavior affected by a change using the documented checks and available tools. Report checks that were not run. Do not weaken acceptance conditions to hide a failure.

Use original or appropriately licensed assets and record attribution in public/assets/credits.md. Do not commit credentials or local environment files.

At a completed milestone, update docs/progress.md with the revision, evidence, known issues, and next step. Follow the user's existing authorization for commits, pushes, and publication; repository instructions do not grant new external permissions.

An optional skill with project knowledge

The example below contributes Signal Garden’s unusual boundary cases. It is useful only if this information is repeatedly missed or if the packaged procedure makes review more reliable. If the acceptance document and an available review skill already cover these cases, leave this sample uninstalled.

READY TO USE · game-review-skill.md
---
name: signal-garden-round-review
description: Check Signal Garden round-state regressions after changing beacon activation, damage, timers, pause, or restart.
---

# Signal Garden round review

Optional example: install only after the referenced game documents exist and these checks add value beyond available review tools. This is not a generic game-development skill.

Use docs/acceptance.md as the authority for current rules and test commands. The cases below describe this book's initial design; update them when the game design changes.

Relevant boundary cases:
- If time expires or health reaches zero in the same simulation step as beacon activation, loss wins.
- Activation requires a fresh E press within two units after all three cells have been collected.
- Drone contact removes one health point, with a one-second damage cooldown.
- Pause freezes both the round timer and simulation. Window blur clears held input and pauses an active round; returning focus requires explicit Resume.
- Restart from paused, won, or lost resets cells, health, timer, robot position, drone progress, cooldowns, effects, and held input, then enters playing for a fresh round.

Select the cases affected by the change. Use deterministic checks for timing boundaries and actual player controls for the affected journey when browser tools are available. Setup helpers may prepare a scene but cannot serve as proof that its controls work.

Output: revision, affected case, reproduction steps, expected/observed result, and evidence. Mark unavailable checks as unrun. Fix in-scope failures and recheck what the fix affects; finish when those checks pass. Update docs/progress.md when this completes a milestone.

To try it, save the sample as .agents/skills/signal-garden-round-review/SKILL.md in the game repository and verify that your host lists it. Keep the referenced acceptance document current. A skill supplies guidance, not browser access; actual tools must also be available.

A small experiment for your Astra setup

This is a proposed experiment, not a result measured for this book. Use the same starting revision, Astra configuration, tool access, game brief, acceptance checks, and effort budget. Keep required policies in place. Try these conditions in separate clean runs:

  1. Baseline: current available skills, with no extra project skill and no forced skill selection.
  2. Selection check: explicitly select the existing relevant skill. This tests whether routing contributed to the problem.
  3. Content check: keep that same existing skill selected and add one explicitly selected, narrow custom skill. Compare against the existing-skill condition to test the additional information.

For each run, record skill availability and invocation if observable, accepted behaviors, regressions, manual interventions, elapsed time, and token cost when available. Score the same playable routes without knowing the condition if possible. Repeat several runs; retain the extra instructions only if their observed benefit justifies their cost. Once content helps, separately test whether its description allows reliable implicit selection.

An instruction audit

For an optional instruction, ask: which observed failure does it prevent, which fact does it add, and where is the evidence? Shorten, update, or remove it when those answers disappear. If an instruction causes a pause or conflict, identify its exact file and rule before changing it.

CHAPTER 07

Design a game worth finishing

A small world can still have a clear identity.

Signal Garden is an original teaching design. You are a maintenance robot on a forgotten rooftop at dusk. Three dormant cells can bring a garden’s beacon back to life. A patrolling drone and a short countdown make the route a decision. The desired feeling is calm exploration interrupted by readable moments of pressure.

The following values are initial design targets. They have not been measured in a completed game. They exist to make the brief concrete enough to build and then revise.

Design dimensionFirst-version decisionObservable check
Player objectiveCollect three cells, return to the beacon, and activate it.A first-time player can explain the objective after reading the start screen.
WorldOne flat 24 × 24 unit arena, with 1 unit treated as 1 metre; simple planters form two routes.All cells and the beacon are reachable without crossing a collider.
ControlsWASD or arrows to move; E near the beacon; Escape to pause; a visible restart button.Diagonal input is normalized; the restart resets all state.
CameraFixed elevated view with a stable orientation; no pointer lock.Player, hazards, and objective remain legible during a full run.
ChallengeOne drone follows a visible route. Contact removes one of three health points, with 1 second of invulnerability.Standing in contact cannot remove all health in a single frame.
Round90-second timer. Win by activating the charged beacon; lose at zero health or time.Win and loss cannot both occur. Pausing freezes simulation and timer.
Visual languageMuted green stone, warm amber cells, a teal beacon, and a distinct drone silhouette.Players can distinguish objects by shape and labels as well as color.
First releaseDesktop browser with keyboard input, responsive menus, static GitHub Pages hosting.The production URL loads, plays, ends, and restarts. Touch gameplay is a later scope decision.

Define the core loop in verbs

Observe → choose a route → move → collect → evade → return → activate. Each verb should have a visible consequence. A cell disappears once, the counter increases once, and the beacon’s appearance changes when it is ready. A hit has clear feedback and a short recovery period. Losing gives an immediate route back into play.

Decide the edge cases before they become bugs

For the first implementation, check loss conditions before allowing beacon activation in each simulation step. If the timer reaches zero in that step, the result is a loss. E should act on a fresh key press, and activation requires the player to be within two units of the beacon. After a terminal result, movement, collection, damage, and the timer stop until restart.

Restart is available from paused, won, and lost. It resets the player, cells, health, timer, drone progress, cooldowns, effects, and held input, then starts a fresh playing round. Losing window focus clears input and pauses an active round; returning focus requires an explicit Resume action. These are our chosen rules, shared by the prompts and acceptance checks.

Pick a single convention for coordinates and units. In the proposed Three.js game, use Y as up and move on the X/Z plane. Keep character speed in units per second. Decide these once in the brief so movement, camera, collision, and tests do not silently use different assumptions.

Give visual references a job

Collect or create references you have permission to use. Describe what each reference contributes: palette, camera height, silhouette, lighting, or UI density. Treat a reference as a design constraint, not an instruction to copy another game’s characters, brand, or proprietary assets.

For Signal Garden, ask for a greybox image first, then a visual pass that keeps the same camera and geometry. Comparing like-for-like views makes the effect of lighting and material changes easier to judge. A more elaborate scene is not automatically a better scene.

Write the exclusions

For the first release, exclude multiplayer, procedural worlds, inventory systems, dialogue trees, and multiple levels. Add one only when it strengthens a playtested core loop enough to justify the extra work.

Check the mathematics behind the rules

For keyboard input (x,z), each component is -1, 0, or 1. Its length is sqrt(x*x + z*z). A diagonal (1,1) has length sqrt(2), so unnormalized diagonal motion is about 41% faster. Divide a nonzero vector by its length, then multiply by speed in metres/second and simulation time in seconds. Zero input must stay zero. This is an elementary derivation, not a benchmark.

n = Math.hypot(x, z)
dx = n === 0 ? 0 : (x / n) * speed * dtSeconds
dz = n === 0 ? 0 : (z / n) * speed * dtSeconds
// At 4 m/s and 0.25 s: total displacement = 1 m.
// Diagonal components are each about 0.7071 m.

This formula is for digital keyboard input. A future analog stick should preserve partial deflection, typically clamping length to at most 1 after a dead zone instead of normalizing every nonzero input. Collision resolution is a separate step: a large displacement can cross a thin obstacle. Use suitable bounded simulation steps or swept collision checks and test the relevant speeds; elapsed-time scaling alone does not prevent tunneling.

For this design, “within two units” means ground-plane centre-to-centre distance ≤ 2; the equivalent squared-distance check is dx*dx + dz*dz <= 4. Use simulation time for damage cooldown and the round timer so pause freezes both. Process damage and elapsed time, settle loss, and only then allow activation if still playing. A single phase value plus centralized transition checks prevents contradictory terminal screens. These are explicit implementation rules for our original design.

Blender study: compare the same scene

These original stills were rendered in Blender 4.5.3 LTS using the shared tool from the neighboring 3d_astra project. They are concept illustrations, not screenshots of a completed game. The neutral lighting makes the material comparison readable; final dusk lighting remains a separate experiment. The dark floor dashes indicate an illustrative patrol guide, not an implemented route.

Rebuild with node scripts/render-illustrations.mjs --blender PATH_TO_BLENDER. The script maps game coordinates (x,y,z) to Blender (x,-z,y), preserving our Y-up convention. Download the editable Blender scene or read the generation script. Blender documents background rendering and argument order. [54]

CHAPTER 08

Make a prompt that makes a prompt

Ask for a better brief before asking for more code.

A meta-prompt is an instruction for drafting another prompt. Its value is the design work it forces into the open: audience, controls, constraints, missing information, completion conditions, and tradeoffs. It cannot guarantee that the generated game will be good. You still need to review the resulting specification and play the implementation.

This step is optional. If the brief already expresses the game clearly, go directly to the compact execution prompt in chapter 9. Use the prompt designer when it resolves a real uncertainty, such as conflicting mechanics or an unsuitable export target. Creating another prompt is not itself evidence of improvement.

Build the input packet

Give the prompt designer the one-page game brief, your target platform, installed tools, available assets, and any existing repository instructions. If the folder is empty, say so. Include a simple reference image or sketch if it clarifies the camera or visual style. Label preferences as preferences and hard constraints as constraints.

For Signal Garden, the important facts are a small desktop browser game, keyboard input, a fixed camera, one arena, three collectibles, one hazard, a complete win/loss/restart loop, and static hosting. “Make something amazing” adds less useful direction than any of those facts.

The prompt designer

READY TO USE · meta-prompt.md
# Design an execution prompt for GPT-6 Astra

You are a game-design and coding-workflow editor. Produce a practical execution prompt for GPT-6 Astra running inside a coding agent. Your task in this conversation is prompt design, not game implementation.

INPUT BRIEF
Use the game brief below or the attached docs/game-brief.md. If details are missing, use the Signal Garden defaults and label them as assumptions:
- Player: a maintenance robot restoring a rooftop beacon.
- Loop: collect three energy cells, avoid one patrolling drone, return to the beacon, activate it.
- Scope: one flat arena, desktop browser, keyboard controls, one complete round with win, loss, pause, and restart.
- Stack preference: TypeScript, Vite, Three.js; GitHub Pages publication after the destination is explicitly authorized.
- Art: original geometric assets, muted green stone, amber cells, teal beacon. Readable silhouettes and camera first.
- Constraints: no backend, accounts, multiplayer, paid APIs, or unlicensed assets. Keep the first release small.

My project-specific changes, existing files, reference images, installed tools, target hardware, and available budget:
[Add these here, or retain the defaults and mark unknowns.]

PROCESS
1. Separate hard requirements, preferences, assumptions, and genuinely blocking unknowns. Ask at most three focused questions only if a wrong assumption would materially change the outcome. Continue independent prompt drafting where possible.
2. Compare only approaches that could change a decision for this brief. Candidates include a one-shot prototype, specification first, tutorial guided, incremental implementation, visual playtesting, and parallel specialists. Explain the relevant tradeoffs concisely; do not invent benchmark results or completion-time guarantees.
3. Recommend a minimal combination and a stack the available tools can actually operate. Preserve an explicit engine choice. Check primary documentation before making version-sensitive technical claims; disclose unavailable browsing.
4. Draft an execution prompt with the player promise, controls, camera, world rules, edge cases, asset policy, verification, and completion conditions. If these already live in accurate repository documents, reference them rather than duplicating them. Use milestones as outcome checkpoints, not a mandatory itinerary for every edit. Prefer available skills; propose a new one only for a specific recurring gap.
5. Include an instruction to inspect existing files before editing, preserve user work, make reasonable routine decisions, and continue through authorized milestones. Treat external publication as a separate permission boundary unless already authorized.
6. Specify only useful evidence: focused logic checks, real-control interaction checks, visual inspection, and human playtesting where judgment is required. Do not claim that a passing build proves the game works.
7. Review the draft for contradictions, requirements without an observable check, hidden extra scope, unavailable tools, and vague adjectives. Revise once to fix those specific issues.

RETURN
A. Assumptions and any blocking questions.
B. A concise comparison and recommendation.
C. The final copyable execution prompt, with unresolved fields clearly marked.
D. A short acceptance checklist and a first playtest plan.
E. A compact explanation of the defects corrected in the review pass.

Keep the final execution prompt self-contained for an empty folder, or explicitly dependent on named existing documents. Use direct instructions and concrete player behavior. Do not substitute another model for GPT-6 Astra, ask for private chain-of-thought, or present a self-assigned quality score as evidence of game quality.
Download .md ↗

Review the result before executing it

Check whether the generated prompt carries the game’s actual identity. If the output could describe any generic action game, the input probably needs a clearer player experience. Then check whether it introduces hidden scope: user accounts, online leaderboards, paid services, generated assets, multiplayer, or a large framework you did not request.

QuestionWeak answerUseful answer
What is the game?A beautiful 3D adventure.A robot restores a rooftop beacon by collecting three cells while avoiding a drone.
What should the agent do now?Plan carefully.Inspect the workspace, record assumptions, then build and verify the first complete loop.
How will we judge it?Make it polished and bug-free.Exercise start, movement, collection, pause, win, loss, and restart; inspect camera and readable feedback.
When does it stop?When it looks good.When the scoped acceptance checks pass, known issues are stated, and the authorized deliverables exist.

Use one refinement pass with a purpose

Ask a reviewer to find contradictions, unavailable tools, requirements with no observable test, and unrequested complexity. Revise those specific defects. Repeatedly asking a model to “make this prompt even better” can produce a longer prompt without a better design.

Version the input brief and the resulting prompt together. If you later change the controls or release platform, update the source brief first, then regenerate the affected parts. Keep a short change note so you can connect an implementation difference to an instruction difference.

A useful prompt review

Underline every adjective in your generated prompt. For “smooth,” “clear,” “fast,” or “beautiful,” add either an example to compare against or a concrete observation to collect. Keep subjective judgments visible rather than pretending every quality can be reduced to a number.

The Astra master prompt

Use a compact request when the repository already holds the detail.

This is an original worked execution prompt for the Signal Garden brief. It is a manually authored example of the output the previous chapter asks for, not a transcript of an experiment or a benchmarked best prompt. Use it in a coding-agent session with the intended game folder open and GPT-6 Astra selected.

Before pasting, confirm the agent can edit the folder, run the package manager, and inspect a browser if you expect automated playtesting. The prompt allows reasonable local implementation choices and asks the agent to continue through the scoped milestones. Publication is handled separately in the deployment chapter so the destination can be explicit.

Option A · the brief already exists

This is the default to try when docs/game-brief.md and docs/acceptance.md accurately describe the game. It keeps the request short by referring to those files. It has not been benchmarked against the longer version; compare them using the experiment in chapter 12.

Use GPT-6 Astra in this game repository. Build the playable desktop-browser release specified in docs/game-brief.md and satisfy docs/acceptance.md. Inspect the current implementation and preserve user work. Make routine technical choices within the brief and continue through the authorized scope. Complete the gameplay, review the running result through real controls when tools permit, and collect evidence for the affected acceptance conditions. Resolve in-scope failures and report anything untested. Treat visual judgment and human playtesting separately from automated correctness.

Follow any existing authorization for pushing and publication; otherwise prepare the release for review with the intended destination stated. Report the delivered revision, verification results, and remaining limitations.

Option B · start from an empty folder

READY TO USE · astra-master-prompt.md
# Build Signal Garden from scratch with GPT-6 Astra

Work in the current project folder as a game developer. Inspect the folder, Git status, applicable instructions, and available tools first. Preserve existing user work. If this is an empty folder, create the complete project described below.

Deliver a small, coherent, playable desktop-browser 3D game. Implement it and run the appropriate checks; continue through the milestones instead of ending with a plan. Make reasonable routine implementation choices and record assumptions. Ask a focused question only if missing information would materially change the result or requires authorization that is not already present.

PLAYER EXPERIENCE
Signal Garden is a quiet rooftop at dusk. The player is a maintenance robot restoring a beacon. Collect three energy cells, avoid a patrolling drone, and return to activate the beacon before the round ends. The world should feel abandoned but recoverable, with clear routes and warm light from restored machinery.

SCOPE AND RULES
- One flat 24 by 24 unit arena. Treat one unit as one metre; Y is up, with movement on X/Z.
- Use a fixed elevated camera with a stable orientation and no pointer lock. Keep the player and routes readable.
- WASD or arrow keys move. Normalize diagonal input. E activates the beacon on a fresh press within two units, only after all three cells are collected. Escape pauses/resumes. Provide visible start, pause, resume, restart, and mute controls.
- The player begins with three health points and 90 seconds. One drone follows a deterministic visible patrol. Contact causes one damage, followed by one second of invulnerability.
- Each cell can be collected once. Display the cell count, health, remaining time, and beacon readiness.
- Use title, playing, paused, won, and lost states. Pause freezes simulation and timer. Losing all health or time ends the round. Evaluate loss conditions before beacon activation within a simulation step so simultaneous expiry and activation result in loss.
- After win or loss, freeze gameplay. Restart is available from paused, won, and lost: reset player position, cells, health, timer, drone route, cooldowns, effects, and input state, then enter playing for a fresh round. Window blur releases held inputs and pauses an active round; returning focus requires explicit Resume.
- Exclude multiplayer, accounts, procedural worlds, inventory, dialogue, and extra levels from this release.

TECHNICAL DIRECTION
Prefer TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js unless the existing project explicitly selects another engine. Use available stable packages and commit the lockfile. Record the actual versions. Check official documentation for APIs that are uncertain or version-sensitive.

Keep a small readable structure with separable input, simulation/state, rendering/camera, and UI responsibilities. Keep tunable values in one configuration module. Use simple collision shapes appropriate to a flat arena; explain a physics dependency if one becomes necessary. Use elapsed time correctly and prevent large resume-time steps.

Create accurate npm scripts for dev, build, and focused tests. Create docs/game-brief.md, docs/acceptance.md, docs/progress.md, and a concise README with setup, controls, target platform, and limitations. Add appropriate ignore rules.

VISUAL AND AUDIO DIRECTION
Start with readable greybox geometry. Then use an original geometric robot, muted green stone and planters, amber energy cells, a teal beacon, and a drone with a distinct silhouette. Keep routes visible; avoid excessive bloom, particles, or camera shake. Shape and text should reinforce color-coded signals. Respect reduced-motion preferences for decorative motion and hit effects.

Use original or appropriately licensed assets. Record sources and attribution. Add modest feedback for collection, damage, readiness, victory, and loss. Begin audio only after user interaction and provide mute. Keep menus responsive and keyboard accessible. This first version targets desktop keyboard play; do not claim mobile gameplay is supported unless implemented and tested.

OUTCOME CHECKPOINTS
Use these to track completion. Adapt the implementation order when dependencies or the existing project justify it.
M0: Scaffold, document setup, build successfully, and display a minimal scene.
M1: Make movement, boundaries, camera, and pause reliable.
M2: Implement cells, beacon activation, HUD, timer display, win, and complete restart from pause or win. Loss remains for M3.
M3: Implement drone, damage cooldown, timer loss, and health loss.
M4: Apply coherent art and sound; inspect readability and feedback.
M5: Test production output under /signal-garden/, fix important failures, and prepare the release workflow.

At each milestone, keep the project runnable, update the progress note, and make a local commit after reviewing the diff and running the relevant checks. Local commits are authorized by this prompt. Treat a milestone as a checkpoint and continue to the next one without an unnecessary permission pause.

VERIFICATION
Run focused checks for single collection, normalized movement, damage cooldown, pause, terminal-state exclusivity, boundary timing, and complete restart. Use real controls in the running browser for the main interaction paths when browser tools are available. Inspect screenshots for camera and UI quality, and observable state for the rules. Deterministic setup helpers may prepare test scenes but must not substitute for journey tests through player input.

Check start, collection, a win, both loss conditions, pause/resume, and repeated restart. Build and test the production output at its repository subpath. Check asset loads and runtime errors. Name the actual browser and device used. If measuring performance, record the device, viewport, scene, warmup, and sample duration; do not invent a frame-rate result.

If a tool is unavailable, complete independent checks, state what was not run, and provide the shortest remaining manual verification sequence. Do not mark untested conditions passed. After a fix, rerun checks justified by the changed behavior; avoid redundant broad testing once the relevant checks pass.

WORKING AGREEMENTS
Keep communication concise and connect changes to player-visible outcomes. If instructions conflict, identify the relevant file and rule and resolve them according to the applicable instruction hierarchy. Use available skills when relevant; no new custom skill is required. If the session permits parallel specialists, use them only for independent tasks with clear ownership and one integration owner. Otherwise continue with one agent.

COMPLETION
Deliver the runnable local game, its source and lockfile, accurate setup instructions, acceptance results, asset credits, reviewed local commits, and a prepared GitHub Pages workflow. Report what is complete, what was actually tested, and what needs human playtesting. Publish only if this session already authorizes the specific account/repository and public release; otherwise finish the reviewable release preparation and request that final authorization.

Why these parts are present

The player promise gives the work direction. The coordinate convention prevents integration mistakes. The terminal-state rules settle edge cases. The milestones make partial progress recoverable. The evidence requirements make completion reviewable. The exclusions keep the first game small enough to finish.

The model-specific portion is short: state how much initiative is expected, how to handle instruction conflicts, when delegation helps, and what test scope is appropriate. Those concerns are reflected in OpenAI’s current Astra guidance. The game rules and target values are our design choices. [01]

Steer the active task with evidence

Do not restart from scratch after every disappointing result. A focused correction should name the current revision, the observed problem, the desired behavior, and the acceptable scope of change. Keep the overall objective intact while correcting the specific failure.

READY TO USE · repair-prompt.md
# Repair one observed game problem

Continue the existing game and preserve the overall brief.

Revision / build: [actual commit or build URL]
Observed problem: [describe what happened]
Reproduction: [starting state and exact input sequence]
Expected behavior: [what the player should see or experience]
Evidence: [screenshot, state snapshot, error, or playtest note]
Allowed scope: [systems that may change and constraints to preserve]

Reproduce the issue before changing code. Inspect the smallest relevant path, explain the likely cause briefly, and implement a targeted fix. Avoid unrelated features or rewrites. Verify the failing sequence and any affected neighboring behavior. Show the evidence for the result and identify checks that were not run. Update the progress note and follow this session's commit authorization.
Download .md ↗

If the agent cannot reproduce the problem, ask it to inspect the simplest relevant scene or add a narrowly scoped observation point. If it proposes another broad rewrite, require an explanation of why a local change cannot solve the problem and a recovery point before proceeding.

CHAPTER 10

From empty folder to game

Finish the loop before expanding the world.

The following sequence is a proposed implementation plan. Each milestone names a runnable outcome and evidence; adapt the order when dependencies or an existing project justify it. Passing a milestone is a checkpoint, not a request for another approval when the remaining work is already authorized.

M0 · Make the project reproducible

Inspect the folder and any instructions. Scaffold the minimal application, record the exact runtime and package versions, and establish the build command. Add the brief, acceptance list, and launch instructions. Start the application and verify the simplest scene loads. If package installation or browser access is blocked, report the precise limitation and complete independent work.

Evidence: a fresh setup can follow the README; the build exits successfully; a floor, camera, and player placeholder appear. Do not spend this milestone on a final title screen or an elaborate component library.

M1 · Make movement legible

Implement keyboard input, a flat arena, collision boundaries, and the fixed elevated camera. Normalize diagonal motion. Browser animation callbacks usually follow display refresh and pause in background tabs: use elapsed time, clear held input on blur, pause the round, and require explicit resume without a large time step. [43]

Evidence: real keyboard input moves the player in the intended directions; boundaries stop the player; diagonal speed matches straight-line speed; the camera shows the playable space. Pause or tab switching does not cause the player to teleport through geometry on return.

M2 · Close the game loop

Add the three cells, beacon activation, counter, timer, and win screen. Keep one authoritative game-state value, such as title, playing, paused, won, or lost. Centralize transitions so UI, audio, and simulation do not each invent a separate idea of whether the round has ended.

Evidence: each cell increments the counter once; the beacon requires all three; activation at the wrong distance does nothing; winning stops the timer and movement. Restart from pause or win resets the round into playing. This is a playable win-loop slice with placeholder art; challenge and both loss conditions remain for M3.

M3 · Add one readable source of pressure

Add the patrolling drone, health, invulnerability window, and time-based loss. Show a readable route and a visible hit response. Begin with deterministic patrol behavior so a bug can be reproduced. Introduce randomness only if it benefits the design, and keep a seed for test runs if you do.

Evidence: collision causes the intended damage; sustained overlap respects the cooldown; zero health loses exactly once; zero time loses; pause freezes patrol and cooldown progression as defined; loss then restart produces a clean round.

M4 · Give the world its identity

Replace placeholders with a coherent robot silhouette, low geometric planters, a distinct drone, warm cell highlights, and a readable beacon. Initialize or resume audio after user interaction, handle playback being blocked, and provide mute. Use the device’s reduced-motion preference to reduce optional motion; a WebGL scene must apply that preference in its animation code as well as its CSS interface. [44] [45]

Evidence: the robot is visible against the floor; the hazard is distinct from collectibles; the HUD remains legible at the target window sizes; sound and pause controls work; reduced-motion preferences avoid unnecessary shake and flashing. Recheck the core loop after asset changes.

M5 · Prove the release path

Build production output, serve it under /signal-garden/, and use the exported game for a complete run. Record a human playtest and fix the most consequential issue. Prepare the public repository and Pages workflow, then publish when the destination and publication are authorized.

Evidence: the final URL serves the expected revision, asset requests succeed, a win and a loss are possible, and restart works repeatedly. The README states controls, build instructions, asset credits, tested browsers, and remaining limitations.

When a milestone fails

Stop expanding the feature set. Reproduce the failure, identify the smallest causal change, fix it, and rerun the affected checks. Update the milestone status honestly, then continue.

CHAPTER 11

Verify the game you can play

A build log cannot tell you whether movement feels right.

Use three layers of evidence. Logic checks cover rules that should be deterministic. Interaction checks exercise the game through its controls. Human playtests judge clarity, feel, challenge, and appeal. Each layer answers questions the others cannot.

Keep the critical acceptance list short

BehaviorTest actionExpected evidence
MovementMove straight, diagonally, and against each boundary.Consistent speed and collision; no escape or camera obstruction.
CollectionEnter and leave each cell trigger several times.Exactly one count increment per cell.
DamageTouch the drone, remain in contact, then move away.Damage observes the 1-second invulnerability policy.
PausePause while the drone is moving; resume after a wait.Timer and simulation remain frozen, then continue without a jump.
WinCollect all cells; activate within range.One win transition, frozen gameplay, working restart.
LossReach zero health; separately let time expire.One loss transition in each case, then a clean restart.
Boundary timingAttempt activation on the step the timer reaches zero.The brief’s loss-before-activation rule holds.
RestartRestart after win, after loss, and after pausing.Player, cells, health, timer, patrol, cooldowns, effects, and held input reset; phase becomes playing.
ProductionOpen the deployed repository URL and play a round.No missing assets or runtime errors; controls work in the published build.

Make invisible state inspectable

In a test-enabled build, expose a read-only state snapshot containing the round state, player position, remaining cells, timer, health, and drone position. Use deterministic scene fixtures to reproduce a boundary condition. Avoid a hidden test shortcut that marks a condition passed without exercising the gameplay rule.

OpenAI’s Astra game case study distinguishes named scene setup from real-control journey tests. Both are useful: a fixture makes a failure cheap to reproduce, while an input sequence checks whether a player can actually reach that state. [04]

// Proposed shape of a read-only test snapshot, not shipped game code.
{
  phase: "playing",
  player: { x: 2.0, z: -3.0, health: 3 },
  cellsCollected: 1,
  secondsRemaining: 62.4,
  beaconReady: false,
  drone: { x: -4.0, z: 1.0 }
}

Define a performance observation

Pick a named device, browser, window size, and quality setting. For an initial experiment, aim for a 95th-percentile frame time under 33 ms during a 60-second normal-play sample after warmup. This is a proposed target of roughly a 30-fps frame budget, not a measured result or a universal requirement. Record loading stalls separately; a smooth average can hide disruptive pauses.

State what the measurement means. Intervals between requestAnimationFrame callbacks describe main-thread callback cadence; they are not a GPU render-time measurement. Keep the tab foregrounded, record the sampling method, and treat background pauses separately. This distinction matters when comparing two runs. [43]

If performance misses the target, collect evidence before reducing visual quality. Compare draw calls, geometry, shadows, resolution, and update work. Change one likely bottleneck, then repeat the same sample. Do not claim an optimization worked because the code became shorter.

Measurement limit: callback intervals measure main-thread callback cadence. They do not establish that every rendered frame was displayed. State the percentile estimator (for example, sorted sample at index ceil(0.95 × N) − 1), sample count, and long stalls as well as the target. The percentile convention is our proposed reporting choice.

Run a small human playtest

Give someone the build and ask them to play without coaching. Observe whether they identify the objective, understand the controls, notice damage, and discover restart. Then ask where they felt uncertain and what they wanted to try next. A small playtest reveals specific problems; it does not establish a population-level success rate.

Build / commit:
Device, browser, window size:
New or returning player:
Could explain the objective? [observation]
First confusing moment: [what happened]
Win/loss/restart observed: [which, with evidence]
Control feel: [player's own description]
Highest-impact issue:
Next change and the observation it should improve:

Separate “I ran it” from “I tested it.” A credible report names the actions, the result, and the revision. If the agent cannot inspect the game, preserve that limitation in the report instead of turning an unrun check green.

CHAPTER 12

Refine the idea and the process

Improve the weakest link, then keep what you learned.

Use the Mermaid improvement loop and decision record to make the cause, experiment, and result visible.

When a first build disappoints, resist adding five new features. Decide what kind of failure you have. A wrong mechanic needs a clearer rule. A correctly implemented but dull mechanic needs a design experiment. A broken control needs a reproduction. A forgotten convention needs better repository context.

A worked prompt refinement

The examples below are illustrative revisions, not measured test results.

VersionInstructionWhy it improves the next decision
P0 · vagueMake a good 3D game with a robot.Almost every design and completion criterion is unspecified.
P1 · scopedMake a browser game in one rooftop arena. A robot collects three cells and returns to a beacon.Defines the world, objective, and minimum complete loop.
P2 · testableUse WASD/arrows, a fixed elevated camera, one drone, three health points, and a 90-second round. Verify win, loss, pause, and restart.Provides concrete rules and visible acceptance conditions.
P3 · situatedAt this revision, the north planter hides the robot. Keep the current rules. Adjust camera or occlusion treatment and compare the same route before and after.Uses evidence from the current build to bound the change.

P0–P2 add specification detail; P3 is a different repair task at an existing revision, not a universally better bootstrap prompt.

Use a rubric to expose disagreements

Score each dimension from 0 to 2: 0 means missing or broken, 1 means present but inconsistent, and 2 means demonstrated under the stated test. Add a note and evidence for each score. The score is a conversation aid, not an objective measure of fun.

  • Clarity: the player understands the goal and current state.
  • Control: movement responds consistently and the camera supports it.
  • Completion: the core loop includes win, loss, pause, and reliable restart.
  • Feedback: collection, damage, and beacon readiness are perceivable.
  • Challenge: the route and hazard produce a readable decision.
  • Coherence: visuals, sound, and UI support the same mood.
  • Reliability: the deployed build performs acceptably on the named target.
  • Maintainability: a new session can reproduce the build and find the next change.

Compare approaches with a fair experiment

If you want to know whether your meta-prompt helps, compare it against a direct prompt from the same clean starting revision. Keep the game brief, model, tools, target platform, and effort budget the same. Record which prompt was used and the actual cost, elapsed time, manual interventions, accepted milestones, and regressions.

Judge the playable outputs without looking at which prompt produced them if possible. Repeat more than once before trusting a difference; agent runs can vary. Do not use a single lucky output to declare a universal winner. If one approach uses extra agents or a much larger budget, report that difference instead of attributing the result entirely to wording.

Keep only improvements that still help

A repeated project convention may belong in AGENTS.md. A recurring procedure may merit a skill when existing tools and documentation do not already cover it. Keep a one-off fix in the task’s notes. Update the game brief when playtesting changes the design. Avoid copying the same rule into several layers by default.

For example, loss-before-activation at the same simulation step belongs in the authoritative acceptance document. A review skill can point to it if the agent repeatedly misses that boundary. “Move this planter two units east” belongs in the current design change. Reevaluate optional guidance after changing the model: a workaround that helped yesterday may be unnecessary today.

The retrospective

After a release, write three sentences: which instruction helped most, which failure cost the most rework, and which single change to the workflow you will test next time. Connect each sentence to an actual observation.

Improve game versions and prompt versions separately

Your proposed loop is useful: build V1, fix it, learn from the prompts, then attempt V2. The correction is to retain prompts plus observed outcomes, not concatenate the conversation. V2 also inherits better code, assets, and human decisions. Its improvement alone cannot establish that prompt P2 beats P1. A prompt revision changes supplied instructions; it does not update Astra’s model weights.

  1. Save a baseline. Record commit, prompt version, model settings, tools and skills, and acceptance conditions.
  2. Build and diagnose. Keep failures, successful repairs, evidence, and intervention count.
  3. Extract verified lessons. Separate facts from guesses; drop failed advice and obsolete requirements.
  4. Store each lesson once. Rules go in the brief; regressions in tests; conventions in AGENTS.md; a repeatedly useful procedure may become a skill.
  5. Draft P2. Reference those files and state the next outcome. A shorter prompt can be better.
  6. Compare when the question matters. Give P1 and P2 the same starting commit, files, model, tools, and budget in separate clean runs. Repeat promising comparisons and include a scenario not used to revise P2. Keep main-game development incremental.

For example, a failed restart should produce a regression check and an acceptance rule, then P2 can say “Implement the next milestone and preserve the acceptance rules.” If P2 receives corrected documents that P1 did not, you have tested an improved instruction package, not wording alone. Decide which comparison you want before running it. This is our experimental design, informed by task-specific evaluation guidance. [52]

Run ID / baseline commit / prompt version:
Model settings / tools / available and invoked skills:
Task / acceptance checks / time and cost budget:
Observed failure / verified repair / remaining uncertainty:
Lesson to retain / authoritative file / supporting evidence:
Held-out scenario / regressions / decision: keep, revise, or stop

A hypothetical change from 6/10 to 8/10 successful runs is 20 percentage points, or about 33% relative improvement. It is not “20% better,” and ten runs do not establish a general success rate. Report counts, failed cases, costs, and uncertainty; avoid ranking prompts by a single attractive output.

The dataset-backed OpenAI prompt optimizer illustrates feedback-based revision, but its documentation now schedules legacy Evals read-only access for 31 October 2026 and shutdown for 30 November 2026. The repository-based method above needs neither service. Optimization can regress on some inputs; verify the candidate before adopting it. [53]
