CHAPTER 13

Publish and close the loop

A release is a working URL and a recoverable revision.

For the proposed Vite game, GitHub Pages serves built static files. It provides no private server runtime for this game’s API calls. A key placed in published JavaScript is delivered to visitors, so keep service credentials in a separate backend or local tool when needed. Signal Garden’s first release needs neither accounts nor an online service. [46]

1 · Configure the repository path

A project called signal-garden normally appears at https://YOUR_ACCOUNT.github.io/signal-garden/. In Vite, set the base path accordingly. A user site at the domain root uses a different base. The repository name’s case and asset filenames must be correct on the deployed host. [12]

// vite.config.ts — example for the game repository
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
  base: '/signal-garden/',
});

Test the production build under this subpath before publication. Prefer imported assets or base-aware URLs. A path that works at localhost/ may fail when the application lives one directory below the domain root.

2 · Build, upload, deploy

In the repository’s Pages settings, choose GitHub Actions as the source. A Pages workflow builds the site, uploads its public artifact, and deploys it with the appropriate Pages and identity-token permissions. Use the github-pages environment and the URL returned by the deployment step. [13]

This book’s actual workflow is a small static-site example. A Vite game should install from its lockfile and run its own checks before uploading dist. Pin reviewed action versions or commit SHAs, and check current official examples when adapting the workflow.

3 · Make publication explicit

After the game works locally, replace the account and repository placeholders in this release prompt. Its publication permission applies only after you actually send it with the intended destination.

READY TO USE · release-prompt.md
# Publish the verified game to GitHub Pages

Publish this project to the GitHub account and repository below. I authorize creating the public repository if it does not exist, committing the intended project files, pushing the reviewed commits, configuring GitHub Pages for this repository, and deploying the game publicly.

Account: YOUR_ACCOUNT
Repository: signal-garden
Expected URL: https://YOUR_ACCOUNT.github.io/signal-garden/

Replace YOUR_ACCOUNT with the actual intended account before executing. If it remains unresolved, ask for the account while completing independent release preparation. Do not guess the destination.

Inspect the current repository, remotes, working tree, and applicable instructions. Preserve unrelated changes and do not overwrite an existing remote repository. Confirm the staged files are intended to be public and include the asset credits. Exclude credentials, local environment files, and unlicensed assets.

Build and run the scoped acceptance checks. Configure the correct project base path. Commit a GitHub Actions workflow that builds and checks the project, uploads only its public production output, and deploys through GitHub Pages.

Push to the intended branch, follow the workflow run for the actual commit, and fix actionable deployment failures within scope. Verify the public URL and production assets. Use real controls to exercise the core loop if browser tools are available; state any remaining manual checks.

Finish with the live game URL, repository link, commit, deployment outcome, and concise verification summary. A queued deployment or a local preview is not the final published result.
Download .md ↗

4 · Verify the public result

  1. Confirm the push reached the intended remote and branch.
  2. Inspect the workflow run for that commit. A queued run is not a successful deployment.
  3. Open the deployment URL and check the production asset requests.
  4. Play a win path and a loss path, then restart. Repeat a pause/resume check.
  5. Record the deployed commit, controls, target browser, and any remaining limitations in the release note.

If deployment fails, inspect its logs and fix the specific cause. For a missing asset, check the base path and filename case. For a Godot export, check the renderer, exported filenames, and browser requirements. For a permissions error, inspect the Pages source, workflow permissions, and repository settings before changing unrelated code.

5 · Keep a path back

Record the last verified release revision. If a new release breaks the game, revert the responsible change in a new commit and allow the workflow to publish the repaired state. Check the resulting live URL again. A rollback command is only a step toward restoration.

The complete workflow

Choose a player experience → compare relevant approaches → verify current sources → establish the repository and brief → use available skills when relevant → choose a compact or bootstrap prompt → build playable checkpoints → test the real game → publish → retain only workflow changes that help.

The durable result is more than a game. It is a process that makes your next attempt easier to understand, easier to review, and easier to improve.

The next two chapters map that process as editable decision and data flows, then apply it to creating a short game trailer.

CHAPTER 14

Think, decide, improve

Make the next decision visible.

A useful thinking flow shows the outcome, the uncertainty, the action, and the evidence that changes the plan. These are observable working decisions, not a reconstruction of a model’s private reasoning. The diagrams below are original proposals for this book. Use them to discuss work with Astra and to review what happened afterward.

Read and reuse the diagrams

Rectangles name actions or artifacts; diamonds name decisions; labeled arrows show the condition or information that moves work forward. A loop means that new evidence may change the next action. It does not mean “repeat forever.” Set a completion condition and an effort limit for an experiment.

These are real Mermaid diagrams: text definitions rendered as SVG. Each includes a readable description, a copy button, the editable .mmd source, and an SVG download after rendering. Scroll across wide graphs, or select Fit diagram for an overview. A diagram explains a process; it does not execute it. Mermaid documents how to embed and render definitions. [36]

1 · The thinking and decision loop

Signal Garden example: “The player loses sight of the robot behind the north planter” is a useful observation. First reproduce that route. Compare a camera adjustment with a small occlusion treatment, then choose the smallest change that keeps the robot readable. Stop when the named route and nearby routes work; adding enemies does not resolve this uncertainty.

Ask Astra for a concise decision record: what changed, what evidence supports it, which uncertainty remains, and what happens next. A lengthy explanation is not a substitute for a playable result. The process can be lightweight for a small edit and more explicit when a decision affects the whole game.

2 · The data flow: prompts, context, skills, and tools

The brief supplies the desired experience. Repository files supply actual rules and implementation. A relevant skill may supply a reusable procedure. A tool performs an action. Results return as evidence for another decision. This separation helps diagnose failures: a better prompt cannot grant missing browser access, and adding an API connection does not settle an ambiguous game rule.

LayerWhat it contributesExample
Prompt / briefIntent and acceptance conditionsCollect three cells, then activate the beacon.
Repository contextCurrent facts and conventionsThe implemented state machine and its acceptance document.
SkillA discoverable procedure or supporting resourceAn available game-review workflow.
Tool / API / CLIThe ability to inspect or actRun the game, capture a frame, or render a video.
MCPA protocol connecting an agent application to exposed tools and contextA server that lets the agent submit a ComfyUI workflow.
HookAn action triggered at a supported agent lifecycle eventValidate a manifest after a relevant file edit.
Workflow engineCoordination across steps, jobs, and waiting statesn8n submits a task, waits, checks status, and stores the result.

MCP standardizes context exchange; it does not prescribe the agent’s planning strategy or make a server’s tools automatically available everywhere. Hooks depend on the host’s supported events and configuration. [23] [24]

3 · Decide what to add

Before writing a new skill, inspect the agent’s actual capabilities. Is the existing skill available? Was it selected? Does it contain the missing knowledge? The skills chapter explains a controlled comparison. Astra’s current guidance supports reassessing overlapping instructions, while leaving room for specialized procedures. [17]

For video work, this question becomes concrete. A Remotion skill can teach composition conventions. A ComfyUI MCP tool can submit a workflow. A hook can check a changed file. They may work together because they solve different problems; installing all three is not a prerequisite.

4 · Improve the cause of the failure

Keep the baseline revision and a short reproduction before experimenting. If the intended rule is wrong, revise the brief. If the code violates a sound rule, repair the code. If the implemented experience is dull, test a design hypothesis. If an agent repeatedly misses a procedure, investigate context and selection before adding instructions.

A decision record you can reuse

  • Outcome: what should the player or viewer experience?
  • Evidence: which route, screenshot, clip, or check exposes the problem?
  • Change: what single cause are we testing?
  • Comparison: what improved, and what regressed, under the same scenario?
  • Decision: retain, revise, or restore; link the artifact and revision.

This record is also a good prompt input. Give Astra the observed problem and the review conditions, then let it choose appropriate implementation details. Save a reusable procedure only after repeated evidence shows that it helps. Next, apply the same approach to an AI-assisted game trailer.

CHAPTER 15

Make a video with an agent

A video workflow can contain skills, MCP, and hooks. The flow itself is a separate idea.

The exact page you saw has not been identified, so we cannot name its software with certainty. A canvas of linked model nodes is often a tool such as ComfyUI. A canvas of HTTP requests, waiting steps, and conditions may be an automation tool such as n8n. An agent calling a media service may use MCP. Below are verified examples and a practical way to choose among them.

A current change worth noticing

Remotion’s documentation, updated 12 September 2026, deprecates its older documentation MCP and recommends agent skills instead. This is evidence of one redundant documentation integration, not evidence that MCP or skills are universally obsolete. Its job was to provide docs; an MCP server that actually submits video jobs has a different role. [27]

1 · Choose the route by the result you need

RouteGood fitWhat you controlWhat still needs review
Remotion + coding agentPrecise titles, captions, UI animation, and edited gameplayComposition code, timing, layout, and supplied mediaActual export, frame timing, typography, and sound
ComfyUI node workflowGenerated footage with visible model and input stagesA compatible template, prompts, references, and exposed settingsModel access, resource requirements, motion, and continuity
Video provider SDK / APIProgrammatic generation and job trackingProvider-supported parameters and task handlingModel variability, cost, failures, and saved outputs
n8n around an APIA repeated process spanning several jobs or servicesRequests, conditions, waits, storage, and review checkpointsRetry behavior, credentials, execution state, and duplicate jobs

This comparison is our synthesis of the current documentation, not a speed or quality benchmark. These routes can be combined: generate an atmospheric clip in ComfyUI, combine it with real game capture in Remotion, and automate a proven repeated process later. [25] [28] [31] [34]

2 · Begin with a small trailer brief

For a first Signal Garden teaser, propose ten seconds at 16:9 with three shots. This is an original storyboard target; no video has been generated for this book. Use real game capture whenever the shot claims to demonstrate mechanics. Label generated concept footage so viewers can distinguish an imagined world from the implemented game.

ShotLengthPurposeSource and review condition
SG-013 secondsEstablish the rooftop and beaconGame capture, or clearly labeled concept footage; the arena is readable.
SG-023 secondsShow the collection objectiveActual gameplay capture; the cell pickup and counter agree.
SG-034 secondsShow the beacon and titleActual activation plus a composed title; spelling and timing are exact.

Make a shot manifest: one record per stable shot ID, with purpose, duration, source type, reference files, prompt when needed, output path, and review status. Record model/version, settings, task ID, attempt number, and actual cost where the service exposes them. This is your project record, not a universal provider request schema. Keep credentials in the tool’s credential store, outside the manifest and public repository.

For a generated establishing shot, try a focused visual prompt: “A small rooftop garden at dusk, a single teal beacon at the center, low planters, muted green concrete, a slow elevated camera push toward the beacon, stable geometry and lighting.” Supply duration, ratio, and a reference image through the service’s supported controls. Add titles during composition. Compare one relevant change at a time instead of replacing the entire prompt whenever a clip disappoints.

3 · Use Remotion for composition and exact graphics

Remotion’s current coding-agent guide scaffolds a project, installs dependencies, previews the composition, and introduces its skills. The commands below create a separate video project; run them in the parent folder where you want that project. Node.js and a working coding agent are prerequisites. [25]

npx create-video --yes --blank signal-garden-trailer
cd signal-garden-trailer
npm install
npm run dev

Check whether an appropriate Remotion skill is already available. If needed, the guide provides npx remotion skills add. Ask the agent to implement the storyboard using your capture files, preview it, and render with the installed project’s documented command. Review the exported video itself. The current skill collection covers composition, documentation, preview, and rendering workflows. [26]

Create motion graphics with AI — Simple tutorial for beginners ↗ is the five-minute companion linked by Remotion’s official guide. We reviewed the written guide; this video’s transcript was not retrieved. Treat it as a visual follow-along resource, not transcript evidence. Its practical sequence is summarized in reading note 25.

4 · Use ComfyUI when you want a visible generation graph

Start from the application’s Workflow Templates browser and inspect the selected template’s model and input requirements. Templates provide a concrete starting graph, while the reviewed LTX-2.5 guide covers text-to-video, image-to-video, and first/last-frame workflows with supported audio. Model access and a compatible installation matter; a new model name alone does not make a graph runnable. [29] [28]

This drawing is conceptual. It is not an importable ComfyUI JSON workflow and its boxes are not exact node names. Use an official compatible template, keep its required model components together, change the prompt or reference input, run one short attempt, and inspect the saved video. If nodes are missing, check the template’s installation requirements before replacing arbitrary nodes.

LTX-2.5 is the current LTX guide reached during this review; its page does not provide a clear publication date. It is a gated model with access requirements. Choose a model your account or machine can run, and start from its supported settings. These are operational constraints, not reasons to copy an older tutorial’s model files blindly. [28]

A local LTX template does not establish that the same model is available through Comfy Cloud. For the cloud route below, discover the account’s actual template catalog and inspect its schema before choosing inputs. Local installation requirements and cloud availability are separate checks. [29] [37]

Let an agent operate it through the official Comfy MCP

Comfy’s public-beta documentation provides this Codex CLI cloud setup, separate from its local connection. Complete sign-in and check your subscription and budget before generation. These instructions have not been executed for this book. [37]

codex mcp add comfy-cloud --url https://cloud.comfy.org/mcp
codex mcp login comfy-cloud
  1. Inspect the registered tools; discover a template with search_templates and inspect its get_template_schema.
  2. Map the brief to supported inputs and confirm the allowed budget.
  3. Use run_template. Custom submit_workflow requires API-format JSON, distinct from editor JSON.
  4. Keep the job ID and wait for completion with tools such as wait_for_job. Use get_output to obtain download instructions. That tool does not write the local file itself: check the destination, perform the documented download, verify the saved file, and review the clip. [37]

Comfy also publishes skills containing workflow and model guidance. That knowledge complements the MCP’s ability to act. Reuse an available relevant skill; add one only when it fills a gap. Its documentation includes host-specific plugin examples, so do not assume a Claude Code installation command also configures Codex. [38]

Repository update: Comfy’s current repository places the canonical cloud commands in claude-code/; its legacy skills/ folder is frozen. The separate comfy-cli now bundles its own skills. Match installation to the host and discover live templates instead of copying old model lists. [55]

5 · Use an API when you want explicit job handling

Runway’s multi-shot recipe, version 2026-06, supports automatic story decomposition or a custom shot list. Its shown schema generates the shots; it does not insert our existing gameplay captures. Use it for a separately labeled all-generated concept trailer. For the mixed-source storyboard above, compose SG-02 and SG-03 from real capture in Remotion. A three-shot, ten-second concept variant fits the documented timing options, but has not been run here. [32]

There is also an important MCP distinction in Runway’s own documentation: https://dev.runwayml.com/mcp serves developer tasks and documentation, while https://mcp.runwayml.com is identified as the separate media-generation integration. Do not configure the developer endpoint and assume it exposes a video-generation tool. Inspect the connected server’s actual capabilities. [30]

Runway’s SDK documentation describes asynchronous tasks and polling. Follow its current polling interval and backoff guidance; its manual polling example says at least five seconds with jitter. A local waiting timeout does not prove the remote job failed or was canceled. Keep the task ID and check it before considering a new paid attempt. [31]

PENDING, RUNNING, and THROTTLED are nonterminal states. A throttled task has been accepted but is waiting for capacity; it is distinct from an HTTP 429 response. For retryable status-request errors, use bounded backoff and jitter. Stop on a fatal error, unknown state, or deadline and preserve the task record. If the initial submission has an uncertain result and no ID, reconcile it through provider records before submitting again. These recovery choices are our proposed orchestration policy. [47] [48]

Save accepted output to storage you control. Runway’s output URLs are temporary, typically expiring within 24–48 hours of access. A task record should point to the saved file as well as the original task, so a later edit does not depend on an expired delivery URL. [33]

6 · Build the repeating flow in n8n

Once one request succeeds, reproduce its working method, URL, authentication, headers, and body in an HTTP Request node. That node makes API calls; the video provider performs the generation. Use n8n credentials for authentication. [34]

  1. Manual trigger: load one approved shot and its allowed attempt budget.
  2. Submit: send one generation request per attempt; persist the returned task ID and shot ID. An uncertain submission goes to reconciliation.
  3. Wait: pause for the provider’s required interval while within the deadline.
  4. Check: GET that same task; route pending, running, or throttled back to Wait. Handle retryable HTTP errors with bounded backoff.
  5. Resolve: save successful output; record failure, cancellation, unknown status, or local timeout for review. A local timeout does not cancel the remote task.
  6. Assemble: use reviewed clips in the timeline, then watch the full export before publication.

The job diagram above is the logic to reproduce with HTTP Request, Wait, and conditional branches. The Wait node can resume after time or through a webhook. Use a callback only when the selected provider documents one, and configure its authentication. A webhook is an incoming HTTP event; it is distinct from an agent’s lifecycle hook. [35]

Keep generation submission outside the status-polling loop. If a request’s result is uncertain, reconcile the existing task before retrying. Workflow recovery should not silently multiply paid jobs. Automating a reviewed small pipeline is easier to diagnose than beginning with a large imported template whose endpoints and models may have changed.

7 · Add a hook only for a repeated event action

A proposed hook could run an existing local validator after the agent edits the shot manifest. That validator checks duration totals, required shot fields, and local asset references. Filter irrelevant edits out. First run the validator directly and confirm that its feedback is useful; then wire it to your host’s supported event configuration.

Current Codex hooks include PostToolUse, which runs after a tool finishes. It cannot undo that completed action. Configuration and trust requirements belong to the host; consult the current hook guide rather than copying another application’s configuration. Hooks can automate narrow checks, while the main agent or workflow coordinates the project. [24]

8 · Give Astra a brief that can become a working pipeline

This reusable prompt asks the agent to inspect capabilities, choose a justified route, and prepare an inspectable first result. Fill in actual paths and the permitted budget. It is an original template, not a measured Astra video-production benchmark.

READY TO USE · video-workflow-prompt.md
# Build a small, reviewable game trailer with GPT-6 Astra

Create a 10-second, 16:9 teaser for Signal Garden in a separate video project.
Target: three shots lasting 3, 3, and 4 seconds, with clear titles and readable gameplay.

Inputs to fill in:
- Game repository and runnable build: [path and command]
- Approved gameplay captures and references: [paths]
- Video project directory: [path]
- Available tools/services and permitted generation budget: [details]
- Publication destination and permission, if any: [details]

Inspect the actual files, installed tools, and available skills. Verify current
official documentation where an API, model, or command may have changed.
Recommend the smallest suitable route: captured footage and Remotion composition,
a compatible ComfyUI template, or a video provider API. Add n8n only if repeated
job coordination justifies it. Explain the choice briefly using the target result.

Prepare a shot manifest with stable IDs, intent, duration, source type, inputs,
output path, and review status. Show actual mechanics with gameplay capture.
Label generated concept footage. Compose exact titles in the edit.
An all-generated multi-shot recipe is a concept variant; it must not replace
shots that claim to demonstrate implemented mechanics. Verify cloud template
availability separately from a local model guide.

Use existing relevant skills where helpful. Do not create a custom skill or hook
unless a missing recurring procedure or useful event action justifies it.
An MCP connection must expose the needed tool; inspect its registered capabilities.

Build a reviewable local composition using available media. If inputs are missing,
use clearly labeled placeholders and list exactly what is needed to replace them.
If no paid-generation budget is supplied, prepare the request but do not submit it.

For authorized generation: validate the provider's actual schema; submit once;
persist task ID, shot ID, model/version, inputs, and attempt number. Wait and poll
within a deadline using provider guidance. Preserve the ID after a timeout and
check the existing job before retrying. Handle all documented nonterminal states
(including THROTTLED on Runway), retryable status-request errors with bounded
backoff, and unknown/fatal outcomes. A local timeout does not cancel a remote job.
If submission is uncertain and no ID was returned, reconcile before resubmitting.
Save outputs to durable local/project storage; receiving download instructions
is not proof a file was saved. Verify the file and record actual cost when
available. Keep credentials out of GitHub.

Inspect each clip, then watch the full rendered export for timing, continuity,
legible titles, audio, and faithful gameplay. Repair the relevant shot or layer
and compare the same section before and after. Report the artifact paths,
what was verified, and remaining limitations. Publish only within the supplied
destination and permission; a local preview is a useful first checkpoint.
Download .md ↗

Review the result and improve the right layer

If a shot communicates the wrong idea, fix its intent. If motion is unstable, change the relevant generation input or choose a different source clip. If text is misspelled, compose the text in the edit. If files expire, fix storage. If duplicate jobs appear, fix orchestration. A longer skill file does not address all of these causes.

Keep the storyboard, non-secret settings, decision notes, composition code, and appropriate asset references in GitHub. GitHub Pages can serve static public media within its hosting limits; it does not provide the worker for long generation jobs or secret-bearing API calls. Review the complete export and confirm the publication destination. [46]

Your first useful experiment

Prepare the ten-second storyboard, capture one genuine gameplay shot, and build a composition preview. Generate one concept clip only if it adds something the capture cannot provide and its cost is authorized. Record what improved the trailer before adding another model, skill, MCP server, or automation step.

Review & corrections

Follow a claim back to its evidence.

Each chapter’s Source check connects its sections to direct references and distinguishes documentation, reported research, interpretation, and original proposals. The reading notes summarize the checked passages and their limits.

This review clarifies Godot export naming, callback timing versus displayed frames, coordinate and distance rules, and prompt comparisons. P0–P3 now identify different instruction stages; game V2 improving does not prove prompt P2 improved. The new GitHub comparison checks scope, dependency layout, and mandatory dialogue. Comfy’s frozen skill folder is distinguished from its current cloud plugin and CLI skills.

Evidence limits: 54 of 55 source entries have checked content. Source 03 remains a historical lead with unavailable transcript evidence. Remotion and GDQuest video transcripts were not retrieved; written guides support those instructions. SkillAlchemy’s Table 5 has a labeling inconsistency, so it is not used as clean transfer evidence. No reviewed independent benchmark establishes Astra game-development gains.

Two original Blender concept illustrations were actually rendered. The game, prompt comparisons, skill trials, and video pipelines remain worked proposals; no Signal Garden game or paid video-generation job was run for this book. The PDF editions include the summary, full chapters, prompts, diagrams, and source notes. Website checks and PDF visual inspection validate the publication, not the proposed game.
